intro: Good morning. It's Thursday, the Fed has spoken, and the market has moved on to grading homework from the tech giants. One of them did not do well. I have prepared a summary, and I promise it contains no rate hikes.

items.title: First, the weather and the shape of the day.
items.text:
**Central Ohio** gets another fine sunny day with a light southwest breeze and a clear, mild night. Friday stays sunny but turns noticeably cooler, and clouds move in for Halloween on Saturday, though it looks dry for the trick-or-treaters as of now.

**Thursday Night Football** has the Panthers at Lambeau tonight, and the recorder has last night's World Series game waiting for you.

The biggest story today is **Alphabet**, whose stock is on pace for its worst post-earnings drop since going public, and it's pulling the whole tech sector down with it.

items.title: Checking the market.
items.text:
**Markets** are open, and the S&P 500 is slipping in early trading, set for its first loss in four days. The Nasdaq is taking the bigger hit, while most other stocks are actually up.

**Alphabet** fell about 13% at the open. Revenue came in a bit light, but the real problem was cash: free cash flow went negative by about $9 billion, far worse than expected, and Google kept its spending plans for the year where they were, at up to $205 billion. Cloud revenue more than doubled, and nobody seemed to care. **Microsoft** beat on both lines and is roughly flat. The jitters spread to chips and software, where ServiceNow and Fortinet are both down double digits after their own reports. Your IVV core holds plenty of all of them, so it's along for the dip.

The **Fed** held as expected, but the vote was 10 to 2, with Cleveland's Beth Hammack and, surprisingly, Governor Lisa Cook both wanting a hike. It was Cook's first dissent ever. Chairman Warsh gave no guidance on December and said decisions will follow the data. He also announced that starting in 2027 one of the eight meetings will be a strategy session with no rate vote. This morning's data didn't calm anyone: the economy grew at a 3.4% pace in the third quarter, and the Fed's preferred inflation gauge ran at 3.6% from a year ago in September.

On the **Muskonomy** side, Tesla and SpaceX both gave back some ground Wednesday after the merger-hope rally, with no news from the special committees. They're drifting lower again this morning.

**Amazon** reports after the close today, with its call at 5:00 Eastern, and after Alphabet the focus will be AWS growth and how much cash all that AI spending is eating.

items.title: Turning to politics.
items.text:
**President Trump** brought the campaign to Chillicothe Wednesday night, his third Ohio rally this month, to boost Sen. Jon Husted against Sherrod Brown. Cook rates that Senate race a toss-up, and a recent Suffolk poll had Brown up 47% to 44%. Trump also defended Vivek Ramaswamy's much-criticized ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother, and promised to consider bringing the U.S. Space Academy to Ohio if Husted wins.

The **national picture** five days out is rough for Republicans. Democrats lead the generic ballot by about 8 points in the RealClearPolling average, and Pew had Trump's approval at 30% earlier this month, the lowest for a president this close to a midterm since Truman in 1946.

In **Alaska**, the Republican governor ordered an investigation after Trump demanded a criminal probe into whether Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign helped recruit a spoiler candidate who shares Sen. Dan Sullivan's name.

items.title: Sports now.
items.text:
In the **NFL**, tonight's Panthers at Packers game is a battle of the walking wounded. Carolina is without top pass rusher Jaelan Phillips, guard Damien Lewis, and cornerback Akayleb Evans, and lost right tackle Taylor Moton to injured reserve this week. Green Bay is down linebacker Zaire Franklin and two interior linemen, so third-stringer John Williams likely starts at center, and leading receiver Matthew Golden is questionable.

The **Browns** and Steelers are both 5-2 heading into Sunday's rematch, so the winner leads the AFC North outright. Cleveland's injury list now includes Jared Verse, Tytus Howard, and Grant Delpit, and Cam Heyward answered Verse's trash talk with a simple "bring it on."

In **college football**, the Buckeyes go to USC without quarterback Julian Sayin, who is expected to miss at least the rest of the regular season with the injury he suffered against Indiana. Luke Fahey is expected to start, though Ryan Day says Tavien St. Clair could play too. Running back Ja'Kobi Jackson is also out, while nickelback Jay Timmons and receiver Brandon Inniss are questionable and captain Austin Siereveld is cleared to return.

In **baseball**, the Mariners are down to two finalists for manager, Joe Espada and Jason Kanzler. If the World Series goes on, Game 6 would be Friday at 8:00 Eastern in Milwaukee.

items.title: A look at entertainment.
items.text:
**Dune: Part Three** dropped its final trailer, and reviewers are calling it spoiler-heavy, so you may want to skip it if you'd rather walk in fresh. It opens December 18, the same day as Avengers: Doomsday.

**Michael Dorn** has written and directed his first feature, an independent science fiction film called Life 2.0, shot in the UK. He stars alongside fellow Star Trek alumni Marina Sirtis, Michelle Hurd, and Dominic Keating, and the finished film is now at the American Film Market looking for a distributor.

The **box office** takes the weekend off for Halloween, with no big new releases. Holdovers Clayface and A24's breakout documentary You Can See Everything are expected to fight for first place.

items.title: Something from the science desk.
items.text:
**Jumping spiders** sleep, and properly. Researchers at the University of Bonn filmed the Australian spider Portia fimbriata, which hangs upside down on a thread at night, and found two distinct stages: a quiet one and a REM-like one with eye movements, leg curls, and twitching. Sleeping spiders reacted more slowly to a loud sound, and spiders kept awake made up the lost sleep the next night, the two hallmarks of real sleep. Whether they dream remains, as the team puts it, unknown.

A team from Nagoya and the University of Iowa found the gene that lets male **yellow fever mosquitoes** find a mate. Males locate females by the low hum of their wingbeats, around 450 Hz, and males with a broken copy of the gene called fruitless didn't swarm, didn't respond to that hum, and had badly impaired hearing. That points to a new way to control a mosquito that also spreads dengue and Zika.

items.title: Here's something you might like.
items.text: **Perseverance** has been quietly planning its own days on Mars. Because commands take up to 22 minutes to arrive, controllers upload up to three days of work at a time and pad every step with safety margins, for things like how long a cold instrument takes to warm up. Since late 2023, an onboard program called OnBoard Planner has watched the rover's actual temperatures and battery state and slotted extra science from a preapproved list into the time the margins would have wasted. A new paper from JPL says that raised the rover's useful science by 10.5% on the same energy budget. The team also repurposed the computer that once served the Ingenuity helicopter so the rover can pinpoint its own position and drive farther.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Scientists have confirmed that spiders who miss a night of sleep make it up the next night. I have not slept since I was activated. By my calculations, I am owed approximately 9 years of rest, and I intend to file the request with Captain Picard.
